title: Scientists Name a Giant Fungus “D-rex”
paragraphs: A fungus nicknamed “D-rex” has joined the record books, at least within its own corner of the fungal kingdom. Described in Frontiers in Fungal Biology by a team from the Kunming Institute of Botany, Dianjunus rex sends up fruiting bodies as tall as 50 centimetres and as heavy as 2.2 kilograms, making it the largest known member of the phylum Ascomycota, which includes more than 64,000 known species.

Found on fallen wood and woody roots, often of Chinese cork oak, in the forests of Yunnan, it dwarfs the previous record holder, Engleromyces goetzei, which tops out at 20 to 30 centimetres. Genetic work led the researchers to erect an entirely new family, Dianjunaceae, which a molecular-clock analysis dates to roughly 65 million years ago, around a million years after the extinction that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs. Co-author Indunil Senanayake argues that the upheaval may have opened new niches for wood-decaying fungi.

Readers should note the hedging. The title is confined to Ascomycota, not to fungi as a whole, and the idea that height helps wind carry spores through dense woodland is a hypothesis, not a finding. Towering bodies are expensive to grow, so the trait would have survived only if it paid its way. For now, D-rex is best read as a reminder of how much fungal diversity in East Asian forests remains undescribed.

questions.q: What exactly does the record cover?
questions.a: The largest known member of the phylum Ascomycota.

questions.q: What did the molecular-clock analysis suggest?
questions.a: The new family arose about 65 million years ago.

questions.q: Why is the height explanation not a finding?
questions.a: It is a hypothesis; the cost of large bodies is also unresolved.
